title: A Dynamic Multiplexing Policy for a Quantum Repeater
authors: Jeroen Grimbergen, Sounak Kar, Michal van Hooft, Conor Bradley, Stephanie Wehner
abstract: We consider a multiplexed quantum repeater that distributes entanglement between two end nodes. Multiplexing is achieved through optical integration of many quantum chips. Each chip hosts an optically addressable communication qubit and a separate memory qubit. The communication qubit serves as an entanglement generation interface between different quantum chips, and the memory qubit can be used to store entanglement. The quantum chips on the repeater are interconnected using a reconfigurable router, which makes it possible to dynamically assign quantum chips for entanglement generation with either of the two end nodes in every end-to-end communication cycle. We propose a dynamic multiplexing policy in which after an entangled link has been established with one of the end nodes, all remaining quantum chips are assigned to the opposite end node. We compare this dynamic policy to a policy in which the assignment of quantum chips to end nodes is fixed. We consider a parameter regime where on average less than one entangled link is generated per end-to-end communication cycle, which is the relevant regime for near-term quantum networks. We show that in this regime, the dynamic multiplexing policy can lead to a significant improvement in fidelity over a fixed policy, while marginally improving the rate. Moreover, even though the dynamic multiplexing policy requires a deeper, and hence, more lossy, router than the fixed policy, it can still achieve higher secret key rates in the parameter regime studied. This makes dynamic multiplexing with a many-quantum-chip repeater especially relevant for the development of near-term quantum networks.
summary: This work proposes a dynamic multiplexing policy for enhancing entanglement distribution in large, many-chip quantum repeaters. By dynamically reassigning available chips after establishing one link, the policy significantly boosts fidelity and secret key rates compared to fixed assignment strategies. This makes it highly relevant for designing robust, near-term quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The paper compares dynamic versus fixed multiplexing policies for distributing entanglement across a quantum repeater node.
main_result: In the near-term regime, the dynamic policy significantly improves fidelity over a fixed policy and achieves substantially higher secret key rates, even with increased router losses.
method: The analysis uses Markov chain theory (including ergodic theorems) combined with discrete-event simulations to compare performance metrics.
model_or_system: The system is a multiplexed quantum repeater node connecting two end nodes, built from many interconnected quantum chips, each containing communication and memory qubits, managed by a reconfigurable router.
key_observables: Steady-state rate, fidelity, and secret key rate (and the Werner parameter).
important_parameters: The relevant regime is characterized by generating an average of less than one entangled link per end-to-end communication cycle.
main_assumptions: Assumes a symmetrically placed repeater node; the dynamic policy requires a deeper, and thus more lossy, router than the fixed policy.
figures_summary: Figures compare performance metrics (rate, Werner parameter) for Dynamic vs. Fixed policies using exact analysis, approximations, and NetSquid simulations, showing agreement under certain conditions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model and problem setup, develops the dynamic policy, performs analytical comparisons against fixed policies, validates results with simulation, and analyzes performance metrics like fidelity and key rates in the near-term regime.
why_interesting: It directly addresses practical limitations of quantum network scaling by proposing an optimized operational protocol (dynamic multiplexing) that maximizes achievable secure communication rates under realistic low-rate conditions.
